extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and educators interested in methods of learning, rhetoric, grammar, ciphering, and pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for treating, teaching, and presenting knowledge: includes criteria for grammar, ciphers, methods of tradition, rhetoric, textual correction, pedagogy for youth, and moral instruction. The page argues what makes different modes of delivery, exposition, and preparation effective or deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of grammar: popular and philosophical
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar's duty is twofold: the popular duty (for speedy and perfect attaining of languages for intercourse of speech and understanding authors) and the philosophical duty (examining the power and nature of words as the footsteps and prints of reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grammar for practical language learning (mother tongue and foreign tongues) and for philosophical inquiry into the nature of words; while some treatment is 'sparsim' and incomplete, it is valuable and worthy to be reduced into a science by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the accidents of words
rubrics_metrics.description: The accidents of words—measure, sound, and elevation or accent, and the sweetness and harshness of them—are important, especially in rhetoric and poetry (in respect of verse rather than argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities have produced observations in rhetoric and chiefly poesy; in modern languages it is as free to make new measures of verse as of dances, and sense (taste) is often a better judge than rigid adherence to antique measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues of ciphers
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtues by which ciphers are to be preferred are three: that they be not laborious to write and read; that they be impossible to decipher; and, in some cases, that they be without suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest degree is 'omnia per omnia' (complete substitution) with a limited proportion of infolding; beware that in practice many matters are carried in weak ciphers because of the rawness and unskilfulness of intermediary hands. Also note wheel-ciphers, key-ciphers, doubles, nulls, and non-significants as forms—choose for practical writing/reading ease, secrecy, and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method as part of judgment: magistral vs probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Method belongs in logic as a part of judgment and comes in two broad kinds: method referred to use (magistral) and method referred to progression (of probation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method determines both how to deliver knowledge and how knowledge is to be progressed in tradition; it should be considered as rules for disposition and limitation of propositions as well as for the architecture of works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver knowledge in the same method as invented
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that is delivered ought, if possible, to be delivered in the same method wherein it was invented; delivering as a form designed for belief rather than examination creates a 'contract of error' between deliverer and receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want sciences to grow (be transplantable), deliver roots and foundations not only the body/shaft; avoid delivering only polished bodies (good for carpenters but not for planters). Beware authors who present knowledge to be believed rather than examined—glory and sloth produce this defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concealed/enigmatical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a method (enigmatical/disclosed) used to reserve secrets from vulgar capacities and admit only selected auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method can be legitimate in some contexts but has been disgraced by impostors who use it as a false light to sell counterfeit merchandise; be cautious of using concealment to exclude legitimate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of aphorisms versus full methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Aphorisms and methods have different virtues: aphorisms condense the pith of sciences and test the writer's solidity, while methods better win consent or belief but are less fit to prompt action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aphorisms cut off illustration, example recitals, and discourse of connection, leaving only substantial observation—therefore only a solid writer should attempt them; methods can appear complete but may secure men falsely. Aphorisms invite further inquiry; methods can engender false complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertions & proofs versus questions & determinations; sparing use of confutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge may be handled by assertions and their proofs or by questions and their determinations; overuse of confutation and disputation is prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confutation should be used sparingly and primarily to remove strong preoccupations and prejudgments, not to encourage disputatiousness; in instruction, keep attention on the main enterprise rather than besieging every small fort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method must fit the subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Different subjects require different methods (e.g., mathematics are abstract, policy is immersed); a uniformity of method forced across diverse matters reduces learning to empty generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow particular topics and particular methods suited to the nature and use of the subject; avoid methods that are the 'husks and shells of sciences' that expel the kernel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation and manner of propositions (longitude & latitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method must consider not only the disposition of argument but the propositions' limitation and manner—each knowledge has a longitude (toward action/particularity) and a latitude (toward other sciences/generalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how far a knowledge should intermeddle within another's province (Καθαυτο) and how particular it should descend: remote, superficial generalities are unhelpful for practice; rules are like unpolished steel-glasses—useful if later filed by practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of imposture-methods (false arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not deliver knowledges in such manner as men may quickly make a show of learning who have it not (e.g., Lullian art, typocosmy collections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These imposture-methods are masses of words across arts that give outward countenance without real understanding—avoid producing or relying on such collections that look learned but lack worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of rhetoric: apply reason to imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of rhetoric is to apply reason to imagination to better move the will; rhetoric fills imagination to second reason, not to oppress it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoric, logic, and morality work together: logic secures reason; morality procures affections to obey reason; rhetoric makes imagination cooperate. Rhetoric's proofs and persuasions must differ according to auditors and their opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt rhetorical persuasion to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective rhetorical application requires speaking respectively and several ways to different persons on the same subject—the political/policy part of eloquence is to tailor speech to auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great orators may lose volubility of application by over-observing well-graced forms; recommend better inquiry into politick application of eloquence and ensure proofs are suited to particular audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for rhetorical impression as well as signification
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical forms that are equal in signification may differ vastly in impression; Aristotle's work on popular signs and sophisms is deficient in number, lack of elenches, and limited conception of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect more forms, annex elenches (refutations), and consider impression (how language pierces or flatly touches) as important as logical signification; examples show that phrasing affects audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory store for speech: antitheta and formulæ
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation for speech should include antitheta (theses argued pro et contra) and formulæ (apt passages for preface, conclusion, transition, excusation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antitheta ought to be brief, acute sentences serving as skeins to be unwound in use (avoid prolixity); formulæ are convenient stock passages for conveyances and ornament—prepare both as a 'shop' of pieces and of ready-made things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for textual correction and edition
rubrics_metrics.description: True correction and edition of authors require caution; rash emendation often does more harm than good (the most corrected copies are commonly the least correct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid altering text merely because a word is unfamiliar; recognize critics' errors where they presume misunderstanding equals falsity. Exercise humility and restraint in editorial emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for exposition, annotation, and commentaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition and explication commonly blanch obscure places and discourse upon the plain; useful apparatus to authorship includes noting times, brief censure of authors, and syntax/disposition of studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotations should illuminate obscurities without over-explaining the obvious; provide readers with judgments to guide selection of books to read and advice on the order of study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical rules for youth: timing, sequencing, and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantical (youth) education needs timing and seasoning of knowledges (what to initiate and what to withhold), beginning with the easiest and sequencing to harder, matching studies to the propriety of different wits, and careful ordering of exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose studies that correct or cultivate particular faculties (e.g., mathematics for inattentive 'bird-witted' children); order exercises to avoid exercising faults into habit; small early training choices have long effects—design early culture carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction for moral knowledge: exemplar and regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral knowledge should be divided into the exemplar/platform of good (describing virtue, duties) and the regimen or culture of the mind (rules for subduing and applying the will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not stop at admirable exemplars alone; they must provide practical precepts and directions for framing and subduing the will so readers can attain and practice virtues in active life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative nature of good: part versus whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing has a double nature of good: as a total/substantive in itself and as a member/part of a greater body; the latter (duty to the public) is often the greater and worthier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and political judgments prefer the conservation of a more general form (public good) over mere individual conservation; use examples (e.g., Pompeius) to weigh public duty over private safety.
